extracted.intended_audience: researchers, graduate students, and practitioners in formal methods, theorem proving, and mathematical logic (mathematicians/logicians/computer scientists interested in proof assistants)
extracted.subtask_description: An overview tutorial on interactive theorem proving: its aims, contemporary systems and frameworks, proof languages, automated reasoning techniques, type inference, and mathematical-knowledge-management issues, aimed at people who want to understand or work with proof assistants and formal verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal correctness (formal proof objects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Working with a proof assistant involves conveying enough information to the system to confirm that there is a formal axiomatic proof. Most proof systems actually construct a formal proof object, a complex piece of data that can be verified independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer systems that produce verifiable proof objects; evaluate artifacts by whether they encode a fully detailed axiomatic proof which can be checked independently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of verification (what gets verified)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal verification involves using formal methods to verify correctness of artifacts such as circuit descriptions, algorithms, networks/security protocols, or mathematical statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about which class of objects (hardware, software, protocols, mathematics) is targeted and ensure the chosen framework and tools are appropriate for that domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability / communicability of formal proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs should provide a communicable 'proof object' and proof languages should map to ordinary proof descriptions where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer proof languages or styles (e.g., Mizar/Isar) that resemble ordinary mathematical prose when human readability is important; when using tactic-based styles, supplement with higher-level comments or structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usability / learning curve
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a steep learning curve (it helps to have background in logic, functional programming, and/or type theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess systems by how much prerequisite knowledge they require; consider learning resources/tutorials and whether target users can reasonably acquire the needed skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Productivity / effort required
rubrics_metrics.description: Verifying even very straightforward facts can be time consuming and painful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure time-to-formalize and amount of manual guidance needed; prefer systems, libraries, and automation that reduce routine effort for common tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical relevance beyond correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal verification addresses only correctness; mathematicians also care about power, natural definitions, interesting theorems, connections, novelty, explanations, and understanding why theorems are true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When formalizing, track whether the formal development preserves mathematical insight or naturalness of definitions; acknowledge that formal correctness alone does not guarantee explanatory value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of formal framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary proof systems rely on a variety of frameworks: set theory (Mizar), simple type theory (HOL, HOL Light, Isabelle...), and (constructive) dependent type theory (Coq).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a foundational framework based on desired features (e.g., classical vs constructive, expressive power, available libraries); evaluate tradeoffs like expressiveness vs rigidity (e.g., Coq's dependent types are expressive but rigid).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of formalization style (tactic vs declarative)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are at least two distinct styles: LCF/tactic framework (apply tactics to reduce goals) and declarative/Isar/Mizar-style that models ordinary proof language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select style according to needs for automation vs readability: tactics can be compact and powerful but opaque; declarative proofs are more verbose but closer to human reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automation for small routine steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Most systems employ automated techniques to fill in small gaps in reasoning. Automated methods do especially well on large, homogeneous problems but often fail to capture straightforward mathematical inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a system's automated tactics/solvers for handling routine inferences; consider integrating domain-specific procedures for repetitive tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain-general vs domain-specific methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between domain-general methods (propositional, first-order, higher-order theorem proving, equality reasoning, combination methods) and domain-specific methods (linear arithmetic, nonlinear real arithmetic, algebraic methods like Gröbner bases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the prover's automated backends to the problem domain; domain-specific procedures often outperform general ones on specialized tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search vs decision procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated techniques can be classified as search procedures (global/top-down, local/bottom-up) versus decision procedures (quantiﬁer elimination, CAD, Presburger, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use decision procedures where the theory is decidable and performance is acceptable; use search-based provers for broader or undecidable problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global (goal-directed) versus local (forward) proof strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Global/top-down approaches (e.g., tableaux) work backwards to construct a proof; local/bottom-up approaches (e.g., resolution) start from facts and reason forwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose strategy based on problem structure: goal-directed methods for constructive/goal-driven tasks; forward reasoning for saturation-style domains or model building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existential witness handling (instantiation strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: When working backwards (tableaux), for existential quantifiers it’s best to delay the choice of witness; more than one term may be needed; all background knowledge is lumped into Γ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay existential instantiation when possible; consider generating schematic witnesses or using heuristics to avoid premature commitments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unification capability
rubrics_metrics.description: Robinson’s theorem: there is an algorithm that determines whether a set of pairs of first-order terms has a unifier, and, if so, finds a most general unifier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the prover’s unification algorithms (first-order, higher-order, pattern-based) and their performance; first-order unification is decidable and efficient, higher-order is harder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skolemization and equivalence-preserving transforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Skolem normal forms and Herbrand forms appropriately; transformations preserve entailment properties (ϕS -> ϕ, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure logical transformations used in automation preserve the properties needed for correctness and completeness of search.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution loop and clause management
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolution-based proving involves generating new clauses, checking redundancies (subsumption), and deleting clauses; issues include how much effort to put into each phase and clause selection heuristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tune clause selection (e.g., biggest/widest/heaviest) and redundancy checks to balance completeness and search-space control; monitor equality handling and information classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality reasoning strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Three strategies: use a simplifier; build equality reasoning into other procedures; use unification up to equivalence. Knuth–Bendix completion tries to extend equations to a normalizing, confluent rewrite system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to normalize expressions eagerly, to integrate equality in the core prover (paramodulation/superposition), or to rely on rewrite/simplifier tactics depending on domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher-order unification considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Second-order unification is undecidable (Goldfarb). Huet’s algorithm is complete; Miller patterns form a decidable fragment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid full higher-order unification where possible; restrict to decidable fragments (Miller patterns) or use Huet's algorithm with caution (complexity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of decision procedures where applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: Many theories are decidable (Presburger, RCF, ACF, mixed integer-linear arithmetic, etc.) and have implemented procedures; universal fragments may be decidable and more efficient and can use certificates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit specialized decision procedures for theories that occur frequently; aim for certifiable results when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifier-elimination method selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantifier elimination (e.g., for (R,0,1,+,<)) gives decidability; practical algorithms include Fourier–Motzkin and more efficient modern methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose quantifier-elimination techniques suited to coefficient domains and problem size; use Fourier–Motzkin for linear real arithmetic and more advanced methods for RCF.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decidability vs practicality tradeoff
rubrics_metrics.description: Decision procedures are often infeasible; undecidability sets in quickly; ordinary mathematical reasoning is not homogeneous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When decision procedures are impractical, use heuristics, partial procedures, or SMT technology; accept partial automation and integrate human guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for combining theories (Nelson–Oppen)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nelson–Oppen: if T1 and T2 are stably infinite and decidable, and languages are disjoint except for equality, then the universal fragment of T1∪T2 is decidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before combining decision procedures, check stably-infinite condition and language disjointness (except equality); if conditions fail, consider alternative combination strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Craig interpolation for separation
rubrics_metrics.description: If ψ1 (in L1) implies ψ2 (in L2), then there is θ in L1∩L2 such that ψ1→θ and θ→ψ2; this can be used to separate combined reasoning obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit interpolation to find shared interface formulas when modularizing reasoning across theories or components.

rubrics_metrics.name: SMT architecture: SAT core + theory solvers
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical combination uses a fast propositional SAT solver core proposing assignments, with individual decision procedures examining proposals and reporting conflicts; the SAT solver incorporates conflict information into search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use SMT-style architectures for heterogeneous problems; ensure the integration returns useful conflict/certificate information and supports backtracking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of automation
rubrics_metrics.description: One wants transparency: one should have a sense of when the methods should succeed, and when they fail, it should be possible to determine why (using traces, or 'binary' checks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer tools that provide traces, proofs, or certificates to diagnose failures and understand solver behavior; avoid black-box automation when verification traceability is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility and adjustability
rubrics_metrics.description: One wants flexibility to get things working again (adding local information, setting parameters, adjusting behavior based on context).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate systems by how easily users can add lemmas/hints, tune heuristics, or change strategies without extensive rework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scalability and experimental evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: One wants efforts to scale; a lot more experimentation is needed with real mathematical contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess performance on realistic libraries and large developments; encourage empirical evaluation and benchmarks (e.g., TPTP, SMT-COMP).

rubrics_metrics.name: Guided forward reasoning and module cooperation
rubrics_metrics.description: Guided forward reasoning with limited data gathering and cooperation between specialized modules seems promising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design systems to allow specialized modules to share focused information (type info, inclusions, inequalities) and to guide forward reasoning rather than blind saturation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type inference robustness
rubrics_metrics.description: Type inference must infer not only types but information from type considerations (embeddings, structure hierarchies, reuse of notation/definitions/facts); it's used both on parsing expressions and applying lemmas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement mechanisms (implicit arguments, coercions, canonical structures/type classes) to avoid verbosity and to infer both data and facts; test on algebraic hierarchies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type-inference mechanisms (Coq features)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanisms for type inference: implicit arguments, coercions, canonical structures (or type classes), and using computational interpretation (unfolding/simplifying) as needed. Coq: expressive dependent type theory, constructive logic, every term has computational interpretation, type checking decidable but rigid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing/formalizing in Coq, make use of implicit args, coercions and canonical structures to make developments terse and flexible; be mindful of rigidity and decidability constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for dependent types (expressiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependent types allow types to depend on parameters (e.g., list A n, Zmod n, Rvec n). Dependent product and sum generalize A→B and A×B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dependent types when encoding mathematical objects parameterized by values; ensure users understand the increased expressiveness and potential complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical structures and instance resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Canonical structures register hints (e.g., IntGroup) to help type inference solve equations like carrier ? = int; they let type inference view particular structures as instances of classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design libraries to register canonical structures (or type-class instances) to ease unification and implicit inference across hierarchies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Library design and type-inference integration
rubrics_metrics.description: In large libraries (e.g., finite group library), type inference is used to recognize decidable equality, define big operations, mediate between sets and structures, manage class inclusions and algebraic constructions, infer views, and mediate between functions and morphisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure libraries to support implicit views and coercions; document conventions and canonical instances to enable automatic inference and reuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical knowledge management (interoperability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Translating theorems between provers is challenged by different foundational frameworks, axiomatic bases, definitions, side conditions (e.g., x/0), and very large proof terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning interoperability, record precise definitions, side-conditions, and proof-carrying artifacts; prefer canonical representations and consider translation layers or intermediate languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting lemmas for automated provers (lemma selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deciding which theorems from a library should be sent to a resolution theorem prover can be addressed with machine learning (Larry Paulson, Josef Urban).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lemma-selection tools and machine-learning guidance to pick relevant facts for automated backends; classify lemmas by intended use (simplifier, canonical proof of equality, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classifying facts for intended usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Register the fact that certain facts are meant to be used in certain ways (e.g., x + 0 = x as a simplification rule; set equality characterization used in some contexts but not others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotate or tag facts with roles (simplifier, rewrite rule, canonical equality) so automated procedures treat them appropriately and avoid performance/semantic pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflection for reasoning about computation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reﬂection is an important mechanism, allowing one to internalize computation and reason about/verify mathematical computation within the system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reflection to obtain efficient, verifiable computation inside the proof assistant, thereby avoiding large trusted code bases; carefully design reflected procedures and prove their soundness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical foundations requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Continued success will require more theoretical advances; we need entirely new logical theories to address conceptual problems and scale formal verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance practical engineering and theoretical research; track how conceptual advances (e.g., new typing or logical frameworks) could alleviate current bottlenecks.
